source: Brit and Hamlet are wed before a crowd of hundreds. As Hamlet stands at the altar, his hands intertwined with hers, he looks out into the crowd.
He is searching for something, scanning faces. And then his eyes find mine, and he smiles a small, sad smile.
Autumn turns to winter. I walk the gardens daily even still. I don't mind the cold.
One morning, I am surprised to come across a soldier climbing out of the frozen pond near the grounds. He did not know the path's extent, and the ice split beneath his feet.
Without thinking, I strip myself of my cloak and surcoat and with my meager weight pull him as far up the bank as I can. His feet find purchase, and he stumbles up onto the shore.
Safely back in the great hall, warming his calloused fingers before the fire, he introduces himself as 'Ferdinand' and asks my name.
But I have seen the sigil of the Norwegian crown on the front of his tunic, so I refuse to give it. He is plenty warm. I leave him there, alone.
Still, he comes to see me the next day, and the day after that, and every day for weeks. Always strolling around the grounds. What kind of soldier has so much free time?
When he sees me reading on a bench, he brings me books of Norwegian poetry. When he hears me humming, he asks me to sing for him. He is a flatterer, this Ferdinand.
But I cannot help myself. I find his simple infatuation endearing. One morning, my father sees us out on a stroll, and he freezes up in surprise.
'Ophelia!' He says to me later, pulling me aside. 'When did you become acquainted with King Fortinbras's brother, pray tell?'
Fortinbras's brother? Not just Ferdinand. Prince Ferdinand. That he kept it secret is not surprising given his unpretentious nature. Perhaps he never considered it.
Prince Ferdinand, as it turns out, came to Elsinore to support his brother in the unification effort. I don't want to love another politician, so I guard my heart against him.
But slowly, winter turns to spring, and each time Ferdinand comes to take me for a walk, I find my resolve... weakening.
When February comes, he asks my father for my hand in marriage. My father, of course, turns to me. 'I like him, Father,' I say, laughing. 'Truly, I do.'
Fortinbras cares not whether his brother marries beneath his station. The relationship between our three nations is ironclad. He gladly grants us his blessing.
By the time the flowers are blooming, Ferdinand and I marry in the grounds we love so dearly. Neither of us was ever much for the church. Some find it scandalous. We don't mind.
But now the future lies before us. Ferdinand was never meant to stay in Elsinore. Now he makes preparations to go to Kalmar, to assist in Sweden's integration.
He demands my father and brother stay behind. After all, they remain far more loyal that faded old world than I do. They belong in Elsinore.
Ferdinand assures me that Kalmar is not so different-- another country, yes, but very alike. And so we pack our things, and one month after our wedding day, we set forth.
I have to believe that the world I'm leaving behind is a strong one. At the same time, leaving Elsinore with a man who knows little of my old life is... strange.
I come close to telling him of those lost days I spent, when time repeated over and over again, when I thought I was going mad.
But he wouldn't understand. No one could. Time to close this book of horrors and open a new one with fresh, unyellowed pages.
And I left others behind. Father. Laertes. It feels as though the closing of my old life has cut me in two.
But it's time to abandon the old and grow the new. Only by forgetting the dead do we have a chance at reaching for life.

This world wishes I had died. That was my original fate.
I could accept the way things were meant to be.
A simple fate. One where I follow the story to its end.

My family and I could leave Elsinore behind forever.
We are utterly without land, coffers, or a way to get by.
But at least we'd have each other.

If I sat on the throne, I could create nearly any world I liked.
But that sort of power comes with a price.

I was always meant to rise beyond this world.
Besides, there isn't a way back. Not anymore.
Not after what I've done.

Hamlet will make a good King... with me at his side, that is.
Still, this world would cost me my family.
The heaviest price at all.

I have the power to create the perfect world.
It might exist only in my mind, but it'd be real to me.
Some call it insanity. I call it closure.

No, Quince. You may not leave. Not now. Not ever.
I'm not your prisoner anymore. You're mine.
Let's both live out eternity in this hell.

Fortinbras's assault was repelled... for now.
But the fires of war cannot be so easily doused.

source: How now, spirit! Whither wander you?
Ah. Quince.
You sound terribly glum.
It's been a long time since I thought about Elsinore. But I find myself wanting to return.
Oh, dear. I thought this might happen.
You could do it if you liked. You are a powerful author in your own right, now.
But you wrote the fate you wanted to see. You used the power I gave you.
We've been all over the universe, haven't we? And there are a thousand worlds more to see still!
What is there to possibly look at in that dusty old box anymore?
I suppose you're right. There's nothing for me there. Certainly I don't care to see any of them.
Well, you can look at the empty castle, if you like.
You have the power to resurrect it on your own terms now.
Do enjoy it while it lasts.

source: What happened?
You're here in daylight?
Indeed. It is possible, though difficult, for me to manifest.
I find it most curious that you are still here.
At the end of the last cycle Fortinbras was rebuked. Was he not?
Yes. I had thought maybe if I could keep them all alive, something would change.
A natural assumption, of course. And yet, here you are, and here I am, trapped under the lip of the goblet still.
There exist certain undiscovered elements of this world.
You know something. You always have. Why are you playing coy with me?
Would that I could tell you. These lips are sealed with a far more gruesome power than death.
But that information, created when I still lived, sleeps inside the castle's walls...
In plain sight of all, and accessible to those curious enough to find it.
Begone with you. I have work to do.
Stop! No—Please! I—
Back in my own bed? But...
How is this possible?
I know what I saw. Someone—definitely—killed me.
Again? Killed?
All right. Let's think about this a moment. I know I will be killed three days from now.
That gives me time to stop it.
Now that I know that Brit is the one trying to harm me, I can act on it swiftly.
I know there are people in the castle who can protect me. I just have to find them.
At the same time, this assassin... if I can't survive their attack, then what's the point of anything more?
There must be someone who can help me root out this assassin's identity.
His death—I've seen it with my own eyes! And the traitor is my own blood, and my mother... oh, dear God, my mother...
Worms, worms and wriggling earth! All I can see is bile and rot everywhere!
I can't stay here. I can't breathe. I need to go.
I suppose I should at least get up.
What... What just--
That book is over on my table now. How did it get here?
His death—
Go now, Hamlet! Out, out, out, out!
I thought...
I suppose I thought that might have been the end of all this. But it wasn't.
...There it is. What's it doing there? What should I do now?
Had quite a nasty surprise back there, didn't you?
I see you've become acquainted with a good friend of mine.
King Hamlet. I thought he was dead.
Oh, he was. Is. But death isn't quite so linear as all that. As you've no doubt observed!
You see, you both share some unfinished business. As do I.
What business is that?
The same business which keeps you trapped in this world, repeating indefinitely.
And so shall it continue until you follow this thread where it might lead.
Wait. What's happened to Hamlet? His eyes... they're... empty.
Ah. He is, shall we say, on pause.
...You've put Hamlet on pause, haven't you? His eyes... they're... empty.
Yes. Thought I'd buy us a little alone time.
One moment.
There we are.
His death—I've seen it with my own eyes! And the traitor is my own blood, and my mother-- Oh, dear God, my mother!
Listen, Hamlet. Your father's ghost? I've seen him, too.
I believe you, Hamlet. I believe you saw your father's spirit. You're not insane.
Now, tell me: Where did you see this spirit, and when?
M-midnight. On the walls. It was around the witching hour. But how did you--
Midnight, on the walls. That's what he said.
Such a feeble, tender-hearted boy, that one.
I shall leave you to it, then.
You know where to find me. As always.
I'm not ready to make that choice just yet.
Hamlet, you're not going mad, but you need to take a moment to calm yourself.
Ophelia, I--
I know. I know what you saw. Go to your chambers, pause, and breathe.
His death—I see it with my own eyes! And the traitor is—
—Your own blood.
I knew you were going to say that. How did I know? Have I seen this before?
Everything's gone upside down. I need to get out of here. I can't breathe. I can't think...
